title: Encapsulation in Java classes
idea: Encapsulation means a class keeps its state private and exposes only methods that enforce its rules, so no caller can put an object into an invalid state.
points: A class is a blueprint; each object has its own instance fields.
Make fields `private`; change state only through methods that check the rules.
Return copies or unmodifiable views, never your internal mutable collection.
Interviewers check this first: public fields or leaked lists signal weak design.

hero.title: A getter that leaks the real list

steps.caption: `new Wallet()` creates one object on the heap. The `w` variable holds a reference to it.
`deposit` is the intended door: it changes the balance and records the change together.
`getLog()` returns the reference itself. Now `main` and the wallet share one list.
`log.clear()` empties the shared list, so the wallet's own history is gone. No wallet method ran.
A public field skips every check. The balance is now negative, breaking the class rule.
Rerun with the fixed class: fields are `private`, and the getter returns `List.copyOf(log)`, a separate read-only list.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: A public field and a leaking getter let any caller break the wallet's rules.

walk.text: The rule lives only in a comment. `balance` is public, so nothing guards it.
`withdraw` checks funds, but callers are free to bypass it entirely.
The getter returns the internal list itself, not a copy.
A caller writes the field directly. No method runs, so no check runs.
Clearing the returned list rewrites the wallet's history from outside.
Compare both lines of output: the object now lies about its own past.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Private state, validated methods and a read-only copy keep every rule inside the class.

walk.text: All fields are `private`. `owner` is also `final`: set once, never changed.
The constructor rejects a bad owner, so no half-built wallet exists.
Every change goes through a method that validates first, then updates state and history together.
Getters expose values only. `List.copyOf` returns an unmodifiable snapshot.
Trying to clear the copy throws, so history cannot be rewritten outside.
An overdraft is refused with a clear message, and the balance stays valid.

pitfalls: Generating a getter and setter for every field; a setter for `balance` re-opens the hole.
Returning an internal `List` or array; callers mutate it and your invariants silently break.
Storing a caller's mutable list as given; copy it in the constructor, not only in getters.

quiz.q: The getter copies, but the constructor does not. What does this print?
quiz.why: `Item` stores the caller's list itself. Adding to `src` changes the object's state too. Copying with `List.copyOf` in the constructor closes that door.

takeaway: Private fields, checked methods, copies out and in: the object guards itself.
